title: Pyramids of Giza and the Great Sphinx
summary: The pyramids of Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure and the Great Sphinx, built on the Giza plateau west of the Nile in Egypt's 4th Dynasty, c. 2589–2503 BCE. Khufu's Great Pyramid is the only ancient wonder still standing.
card: Giza holds the tombs of three 4th Dynasty kings: Khufu's Great Pyramid, about 146.7 m tall and 230.3 m a side as Flinders Petrie surveyed it, and the smaller pyramids of Khafre and Menkaure, with the Sphinx cut from bedrock beside Khafre's valley temple. Papyri from Khufu's Red Sea harbour at Wadi al-Jarf and the excavated builders' town of Heit el-Ghurab show how the state shipped stone and fed its workers. Most of the fine limestone casing was stripped in the Middle Ages.
what:
The Giza pyramid field stands on a limestone plateau on the west bank of the Nile, at the northern end of the necropolis of ancient Memphis. It is one part of the UNESCO World Heritage property Memphis and its Necropolis – the Pyramid Fields from Giza to Dahshur, inscribed in 1979. Three kings of the 4th Dynasty were buried here: Khufu (Greek Cheops), his son Khafre (Chephren) and his grandson Menkaure (Mycerinus). Each pyramid was the centre of a complex that also had a valley temple near the water, a causeway, an upper temple for the king's cult, small queens' and satellite pyramids, boat burials, and the mastaba tombs of relatives and officials.

Khufu's pyramid, which the Egyptians called Akhet-Khufu, the Horizon of Khufu, came first and is the largest. Petrie's survey of 1880–82 reconstructed its base at 9,068.8 inches (230.35 m) a side and its original height at about 5,776 inches (146.7 m), with faces sloping at about 51°52′. By the same survey Khafre's pyramid measured about 215.3 m at the base and 143.9 m high, and Menkaure's about 105.5 m and 65.1 m. The Great Sphinx, a lion's body with a king's head carved out of the bedrock, lies beside Khafre's valley temple, and most scholars date it to his reign; a minority view assigns it to Khufu.

The absolute dates are approximate. Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities gives Khufu c. 2589–2566 BCE, a lower chronology by Hornung and colleagues starts his reign about 2509 BCE, and a 2010 radiocarbon model places his accession between 2629 and 2558 BCE; the disagreement concerns how reign lengths are tied to the calendar, not the order of kings.

The pyramids were faced with fine white limestone shipped from Tura across the river, with granite on the lowest courses of Khafre's and Menkaure's. After men of the caliph al-Ma'mun tunnelled into the Great Pyramid around 820–830 CE, the monuments were used as quarries, and most of the casing was stripped, reportedly for Sultan Hasan's mosque in 1356 among other buildings.

uncertainty.note: Start is the accession of Khufu, c. 2589 BCE in the Shaw chronology used by Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities (astronomical −2588). The Bronk Ramsey et al. (2010) radiocarbon model gives a 95% range of 2629–2558 BCE for his accession; Hornung et al. give 2509 BCE. The range here spans 2629 to 2509 BCE. End is the present: the monuments still stand.

how: Each pyramid was built within its owner's reign; the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities estimates 10 to 20 years for Khufu's. The core masonry was local Giza limestone cut on the plateau, while the finer facing stone came by boat from the Tura quarries on the east bank. Petrie estimated the Great Pyramid at about 2.3 million blocks averaging some 2.5 tons. The most direct evidence for the logistics comes from papyri found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf, Khufu's harbour on the Red Sea coast and the oldest papyrus archive yet found in Egypt. The logbook of Inspector Merer follows a team of about 40 boatmen who made two or three round trips every ten days between Tura and Akhet-Khufu while the Nile flood was high, from July to November in Year 26, the last attested year of the reign, probably while the casing was being fitted. The boats often stopped at Ro-She Khufu, the entrance to an artificial basin at the foot of the plateau, which was run by the vizier Ankhhaf, the king's half-brother and director of the works. On the plateau, the settlement of Heit el-Ghurab, 400 m south of the Sphinx and over 7 ha in area, housed and fed labourers, craftsmen and administrators in galleries, houses, bakeries, workshops and grain silos, with food brought from across Egypt; it was demolished after Menkaure's pyramid was finished. How the blocks were raised remains debated; ramp theories, including an internal-ramp proposal, are discussed by Tallet without being resolved. The Sphinx was carved from a block of bedrock left standing when the surrounding quarry ditch was cut, and its strata are still visible on its body.
why_it_matters: For about 3,800 years Khufu's pyramid was the tallest structure on Earth, and it is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world still standing; Giza already drew visitors in Roman times. It is also the clearest surviving evidence of what an early state could organise. The Wadi al-Jarf logbooks and the Heit el-Ghurab town show the 4th Dynasty court running river transport timed to the flood, an artificial harbour basin, rationed food brought from across the country and a supervised workforce, all for one royal tomb. The complexes kept working after their kings died: Menkaure's valley temple held his cult and a priests' town until the reign of Pepi II. The stones also record later history, from al-Ma'mun's tunnel to the medieval reuse of the casing and Petrie's survey, whose measurements Egyptologists still use. Two counterfactuals show how much survival depends on chance. Had the builders' town not been abandoned and demolished so soon after Menkaure's reign, it would not survive as the short-lived time capsule its excavators describe. Without the medieval quarrying, the pyramids would still have the smooth polished faces that William of Baldensel saw in 1336. Today UNESCO warns that development and urban growth threaten the plateau's setting between the Nile and the desert.

perspectives.holder: Majority view: Selim Hassan, Ahmed Fakhry, Mark Lehner, Zahi Hawass; Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities
perspectives.account: The Sphinx was carved under Khafre: it sits in a quarry he most likely used, beside his causeway and his valley temple, which was finished before work on the Sphinx began, and its face resembles his statues.
The Sphinx and the Sphinx Temple were planned under Khufu as a guardian of the Horizon of Khufu; Hawass judges these arguments unconvincing.

footprint.description: Three square pyramid bases oriented to the cardinal points, from Petrie's triangulation of the rock-cut sockets and casing remains: Khufu 230.35 m a side (azimuth about −3′43″), Khafre 215.26 m (about −5′26″), Menkaure about 105.50 m at the intended base (about +14′3″). UNESCO has not yet published georeferenced boundary polygons for property 86; the plateau-wide footprint of temples, causeways and cemeteries therefore awaits a surveyed source.

casing courses as Petrie recorded them: granite lower courses on Khafre's (two) and Menkaure's (sixteen) pyramids, the surviving limestone cap near Khafre's summit, and the stepped core of Khufu's; the Sphinx's bedrock strata from the AERA/ARCE survey archive where licensed

phases.description: Khufu's pyramid built, est. 10 to 20 years; casing of Tura limestone being fitted in Year 26 per the Merer logbook.
Merer's crew ships Tura limestone to Akhet-Khufu, July–November of Year 26.
Khafre's pyramid complex built and the Great Sphinx carved beside his valley temple.
Menkaure's pyramid built; complex left unfinished and completed in mudbrick by Shepseskaf.
Heit el-Ghurab builders' town decommissioned and demolished after Menkaure's pyramid was completed (exact date not given by the source).
Pyramids stand cased; the Great Pyramid's casing remains in place until the medieval quarrying.
Thutmose IV erects the Dream Stela between the Sphinx's paws; Amenhotep II had built a temple beside it.
Al-Ma'mun's men force a tunnel into the Great Pyramid (dated by Petrie to 20–30 years before an Arabic manuscript of 850 CE).

Casing quarried: William of Baldensel still saw large polished stones in 1336; Khufu's casing apparently stripped for Sultan Hasan's mosque in 1356; Khafre's casing reported in place in 1581 and 1591 but only its present cap shown by Sandys in 1611.
Stepped cores exposed; Khufu's pyramid stands nearly to its original height despite losing almost all its casing.

materials.material: core of local Giza limestone quarried on the plateau
Khufu pyramid: smooth casing of fine white limestone shipped from Tura (Petrie calls it Mokattam limestone)
Khafre pyramid: lowest two casing courses granite, upper casing greyer east-bank limestone; after 1611 only a cap of casing near the summit, as in Petrie's day
Menkaure pyramid: lowest sixteen courses cased in granite (only partly surviving), limestone above
Khufu pyramid: exposed stepped limestone core after removal of the casing
Great Sphinx: carved from the plateau's bedrock limestone, with natural strata visible and later masonry veneer

reviewer_note: Least sure of absolute dates (the Ministry's Shaw-based dates, Hornung's lower chronology and the radiocarbon model differ by up to ~80 years) and of the casing-stripping chronology, which rests on Petrie's hedged reading of medieval reports; present-day height omitted for lack of an opened source.
